set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
set1.q: A junctional rhythm due to sick sinus syndrome or high-grade atrioventricular block is treated with what?
opts: Adenosine blocks the atrioventricular node further and would worsen the problem; a permanent pacemaker is needed.
Ablation treats tachycardias; a junctional rhythm from high-grade block or sick sinus syndrome needs a permanent pacemaker.
Correct. If a junctional rhythm is due to complete or high-grade atrioventricular block or to sick sinus syndrome, a permanent pacemaker is placed.
Observation suits an asymptomatic healthy person; junctional rhythm from high-grade block or sick sinus syndrome needs a permanent pacemaker.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Why is adenosine useful when focal atrial tachycardia is suspected?
opts: Adenosine is usually less effective at terminating focal atrial tachycardia than nodal or accessory pathway reentry; that relative failure, not reliable termination, is what makes it diagnostic.
The usual cure for focal atrial tachycardia is catheter ablation, which succeeds in about 90%; adenosine is a diagnostic tool.
Adenosine acts for seconds and has no preventive role; chronic focal atrial tachycardia is managed with oral rate control or ablation.
Correct. Adenosine is an important diagnostic tool because it is usually less effective at terminating focal atrial tachycardia than the reentry tachycardias that depend on the atrioventricular node.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Which is a listed risk factor for atrial fibrillation?
opts: Correct. Atrial fibrillation is commonly seen with hypertension, diabetes, cardiac disease, family history of atrial fibrillation, obesity, sleep apnea, excessive alcohol and older age.
Hypothyroidism is listed as a cause of sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome, not among the atrial fibrillation risks.
Obesity, not low body weight, is the listed weight-related risk factor; the others are hypertension, diabetes, cardiac disease, family history, sleep apnea, excessive alcohol and older age.
Atrial fibrillation is commonly seen in the elderly, so older age, not youth, is the listed age risk; sleep apnea, obesity, hypertension and diabetes are on the list too.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: What is the first-line treatment for stable supraventricular tachycardia?
opts: Adenosine is second, given if a vagal maneuver fails in stable supraventricular tachycardia, and it may be repeated once.
Immediate synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia; a stable patient starts with a vagal maneuver.
Procainamide is for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, where adenosine must be avoided; stable supraventricular tachycardia starts with a vagal maneuver.
Correct. Stable supraventricular tachycardia is treated first with a vagal maneuver, then adenosine (which may be repeated once); an unstable patient gets immediate synchronized cardioversion.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: A slow sinus rhythm that is causing hypotension and confusion is treated first with which drug?
opts: Metoprolol is a beta blocker, and beta blockers are a listed cause of sinus bradycardia; giving one would worsen the problem.
Digoxin is a listed drug cause of sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome, so it would slow the heart further rather than rescue it.
Correct. Acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia is treated first with atropine, then a temporary pacemaker if it fails; chronic symptomatic disease needs a permanent pacemaker.
Adenosine blocks the atrioventricular node to stop supraventricular tachycardia; in a slow, unstable rhythm it would deepen the bradycardia.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: In tachy-brady syndrome, which tachyarrhythmia is most common?
opts: Atrial flutter is a fast atrial rhythm, but it is not the usual tachyarrhythmia of tachy-brady syndrome; atrial fibrillation is.
Ventricular tachycardia can be the fast rhythm in some patients, who then need a pacemaker with a defibrillator, but atrial fibrillation is the most common.
In tachy-brady syndrome the fast rhythm comes from outside the failing sinus node, most commonly atrial fibrillation, not a sinus tachycardia.
Correct. In tachy-brady syndrome a tachyarrhythmia, most commonly atrial fibrillation, alternates with symptomatic bradycardia or with offset pauses.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: What is the usual rate of atrial fibrillation?
opts: 40 to 60 is the usual rate of a junctional rhythm; atrial fibrillation usually runs at 110 to 160 beats per minute, irregularly irregular.
A rate of 60 to 100 is the normal sinus range; atrial fibrillation usually runs faster, at 110 to 160 beats per minute, and irregularly irregular.

Correct. Atrial fibrillation usually runs at 110 to 160 beats per minute, although the rate can fall below 80 or rise above 200; the rhythm is irregularly irregular with absent P waves and a narrow QRS.
250 to 300 is the atrial rate of the sawtooth waves in atrial flutter; the counted rate in atrial fibrillation is usually 110 to 160.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
set1.q: In whom are the symptoms of supraventricular tachycardia more pronounced?
opts: Correct. Symptoms of supraventricular tachycardia, such as palpitations, dyspnea and chest discomfort, may be more pronounced in the elderly and in those with underlying structural heart disease.
Young people without heart disease tend to tolerate supraventricular tachycardia better; symptoms are more pronounced in the elderly or with structural disease.
Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia may cause only transient symptoms; it is older age and structural heart disease, not the paroxysmal pattern, that make symptoms more pronounced.
Women outnumber men in atrioventricular nodal reentry, but symptom severity is linked to older age and structural heart disease, not sex.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Which physical finding fits atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia?
opts: Absent leg pulses point to arterial occlusion; the examination clue in nodal reentry is visible neck pulsations.
Correct. Patients typically complain of sudden-onset palpitations and neck pulsations, seen on examination as the frog sign.
Kussmaul sign, a jugular venous pressure that rises with inspiration, points to constrictive pericarditis, not a nodal reentry tachycardia.
Pulsus paradoxus, an exaggerated drop in systolic pressure on inspiration, is a feature of cardiac tamponade.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: What defines long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation?
opts: Continuous for 7 days to a year
Continuous atrial fibrillation for more than 7 days but less than one year is persistent; it becomes long-standing persistent only after more than a year.
Episodes lasting under a week that usually end without treatment are paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, not long-standing persistent, which is continuous for over a year.
A joint decision by patient and clinician to stop restoring sinus rhythm defines permanent atrial fibrillation, not long-standing persistent, which is defined by duration.

Correct. Long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation is continuous for more than one year; persistent is more than 7 days but less than a year, and permanent is defined by a joint decision, not by duration.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia is more common in whom?
opts: Men are less often affected; atrioventricular nodal reentry is far more common in women than in men.
Severe chronic lung disease is the setting of multifocal atrial tachycardia; nodal reentry favors women without heart disease.
Prior heart surgery and atrial scarring set up atrial flutter or sick sinus syndrome; nodal reentry favors women with normal hearts.
Correct. Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia affects women far more than men, commonly without heart disease, spontaneously or with exertion, caffeine or alcohol.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
set1.q: How is a junctional rhythm generally tolerated?
opts: Correct. A junctional rhythm is generally well tolerated; management depends on the cause, from no treatment in a healthy person to a pacemaker for block or sick sinus syndrome.
Syncope is not the usual course; a junctional rhythm is generally well tolerated at 40 to 60.
A junctional rhythm is not a precursor of ventricular fibrillation; it is generally well tolerated, and a healthy person needs no treatment.
Only junctional rhythm from high-grade block or sick sinus syndrome needs a pacemaker; it is generally well tolerated.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
set1.q: Which is a listed cause of junctional rhythm?
opts: Anemia causes a compensatory sinus tachycardia; junctional rhythm follows sinus node failure, inferior infarction, surgery or digoxin toxicity.
Correct. Causes of junctional rhythm include sinus node dysfunction or marked bradycardia, inferior myocardial infarction, the acute period after cardiac surgery and digoxin toxicity.
Hyperthyroidism speeds the sinus node and causes sinus tachycardia; junctional rhythm appears when the sinus node fails or with digoxin toxicity.
Caffeine triggers nodal reentry and premature atrial beats, not a slow junctional rhythm.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: For stable, symptomatic focal atrial tachycardia, which acute drugs are used?
opts: Atropine speeds the sinus node and is first line for unstable bradycardia, the opposite of what a fast atrial focus needs.
Intravenous magnesium is the treatment for torsades de pointes; stable focal atrial tachycardia gets a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.
Procainamide is the drug for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; focal atrial tachycardia is rate-controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.

Correct. Hemodynamically stable, symptomatic focal atrial tachycardia is treated with an intravenous beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, while the precipitating cause is found and treated.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Besides drugs and thyroid disease, which condition is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia?
opts: Pain and anxiety cause a physiologic sinus tachycardia, the normal response to stress, rather than bradycardia.
Hypoxia is listed among the pathologic causes of sinus tachycardia; the bradycardic causes include raised intracranial pressure and sinus node ischemia.
Correct. Increased intracranial pressure is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, together with sinus node ischemia, late-stage infection, hypothyroidism and the rate-slowing drugs.
Pulmonary embolism is a pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia, along with hypoxia, shock and myocardial infarction; it does not slow the sinus node.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: What QRS does orthodromic reentrant tachycardia produce?
opts: Correct. In orthodromic reentry the impulse goes down the atrioventricular node and back up the accessory pathway, giving a regular narrow complex tachycardia with no delta wave and a retrograde P wave after the QRS.
A wide QRS with a delta wave is antidromic reentry, where the ventricles are activated down the accessory pathway.
Wide and bizarre, no P wave
An early wide, bizarre QRS with no P wave is a premature ventricular contraction, not orthodromic reentry.
A narrow QRS with sawtooth waves is atrial flutter; orthodromic reentry has no flutter waves.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Which condition is a pathologic cause of sinus bradycardia?
opts: Hypovolemia causes a pathologic sinus tachycardia as the heart compensates for a low circulating volume; it does not cause bradycardia.
Correct. Hypothyroidism is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, with sinus node ischemia, increased intracranial pressure, late-stage infection and drugs such as beta blockers and digoxin.
Hyperthyroidism is a pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia; it is the underactive thyroid that slows the sinus rate.
Anemia drives a compensatory sinus tachycardia, like hypovolemia and hypoxia, rather than slowing the heart.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Persistent, symptomatic premature atrial contractions are treated first with which?
opts: Amiodarone is used to cardiovert focal atrial tachycardia; persistent premature atrial contractions are treated with a beta blocker.

Correct. Persistent, symptomatic premature atrial contractions are treated with a beta blocker such as metoprolol if not contraindicated, or ablation when they are frequent or trigger atrial fibrillation.
Adenosine terminates supraventricular tachycardia for seconds; it is not used to suppress premature atrial beats.
Procainamide is for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; symptomatic premature atrial beats get a beta blocker.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: In sinus arrhythmia, how does the heart rate change with breathing?
opts: A changing P-wave shape with an irregular rate suggests multifocal atrial tachycardia. Sinus arrhythmia keeps uniform P waves while the rate follows breathing.
Faster on inspiration, slower on expiration
Correct. Sinus arrhythmia is irregular with a pattern: the sinus rate speeds up with inspiration and slows with expiration, while every beat keeps a normal P wave and narrow QRS.
Slower on inspiration, faster on expiration
This reverses the pattern. In sinus arrhythmia the sinus rate rises during inspiration and falls during expiration.
Faster in both phases of the breath
The rate does not rise throughout the breath; it rises with inspiration and slows with expiration, which is what makes the rhythm irregular with a pattern.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: How is hemodynamically stable atrial flutter treated first?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable flutter; the stable patient starts with rate control.
Ablation is the definitive management of flutter, chosen for recurrence rather than as the first step; a stable patient starts with rate control using a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.
Adenosine is used for supraventricular tachycardia; stable flutter is rate-controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.
Correct. Stable atrial flutter is rate-controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker; an unstable patient gets synchronized cardioversion.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Which drug is a direct oral anticoagulant preferred in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation?
opts: Procainamide is an antiarrhythmic used in atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; it does not prevent clots.
Correct. Apixaban is one of the direct oral anticoagulants preferred in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, with dabigatran, edoxaban and rivaroxaban.
Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist used as an alternative with a target international normalized ratio of 2 to 3; it is not a direct oral anticoagulant.
Aspirin is an antiplatelet drug, not an anticoagulant; the preferred agents are direct oral anticoagulants such as apixaban.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Adenosine slows a tachycardia and reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. Which drug is used?
opts: Atropine speeds the heart and treats unstable bradycardia; it would worsen a pre-excited tachycardia, which needs procainamide.
Magnesium is for torsades de pointes; pre-excited atrial fibrillation is treated with procainamide.

Correct. When slowing from adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, intravenous procainamide is used and adenosine is not repeated; adenosine and the other nodal blockers leave the accessory pathway unopposed.
More adenosine blocks only the normal atrioventricular node and leaves the accessory pathway to carry the fibrillation; procainamide is used.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: What defines inappropriate sinus tachycardia?
opts: A fast rate from fever or infection is a response to a pathologic process, which makes it appropriate; inappropriate tachycardia has no explanation.
Exercise tachycardia is a normal physiologic response; inappropriate sinus tachycardia persists with no cause found.
A medication or stimulant effect is an explained, appropriate sinus tachycardia; inappropriate means no cause remains after all are excluded.
Correct. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is an elevated heart rate that remains unexplained after secondary causes have been excluded, so it is a diagnosis of exclusion.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: What is the tachy-brady form of sick sinus syndrome?
opts: Slowing on expiration, speeding up on inspiration
Rate change with breathing is sinus arrhythmia, a normal variant; tachy-brady syndrome alternates a tachyarrhythmia with bradycardia or pauses.
Fast atrial rhythms alternating with slow ones

Correct. In tachy-brady syndrome a tachyarrhythmia, most commonly atrial fibrillation, alternates with symptomatic bradycardia or offset pauses; fast atrial rhythms alternate with slow rhythms or pauses.
An impulse that cannot exit the node
An impulse that forms but cannot exit the sinus node is sinus node exit block, a different form of sick sinus syndrome.
An impulse the node fails to generate
An impulse that is never generated is sinus arrest, which may let a junctional rhythm take over; tachy-brady is fast alternating with slow.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Which medication class is a recognized cause of sinus bradycardia?
opts: Stimulants are a drug cause of sinus tachycardia, not bradycardia; the bradycardic drugs are beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin.
Beta-agonists can precipitate atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia, a fast rhythm; beta blockers, not beta-agonists, slow the sinus rate.

Correct. Beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin are the medication causes of sinus bradycardia, alongside hypothyroidism, sinus node ischemia and raised intracranial pressure.
Anticholinergic drugs cause sinus tachycardia, as stimulants do; they block the vagal brake rather than slowing the sinus node.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
set1.q: What is the usual rate of a junctional rhythm?
opts: Correct. A junctional rhythm is regular, usually at 40 to 60 beats per minute, with a narrow QRS and P waves that are inverted, buried or after the QRS.
60 to 100 is the normal sinus rate; a junctional rhythm is slower, usually 40 to 60 beats per minute.
100 to 160 is the range of sinus tachycardia; a junctional rhythm usually runs at 40 to 60.
250 to 300 is the atrial rate of flutter; the junction usually paces at 40 to 60.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Which counseling fits benign premature atrial contractions?
opts: Anticoagulation belongs to atrial fibrillation and flutter; benign premature atrial beats need reassurance and trigger avoidance.
A beta blocker is only for persistent symptoms; benign premature atrial contractions are managed with reassurance and trigger avoidance.
Correct. Counsel the patient to avoid potential precipitants such as excessive alcohol, stress and caffeine, and give reassurance of the benign nature of the rhythm.
Exercise restriction is not part of the counseling; the advice is to avoid precipitants like alcohol, stress and caffeine, with reassurance.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Which therapy is usually curative for focal atrial tachycardia?
opts: Pacemakers treat slow rhythms; an ectopic atrial focus driving a tachycardia is cured by catheter ablation.
Atropine speeds the heart and is used for unstable bradycardia; it has no role in curing focal atrial tachycardia.
Correct. Catheter ablation of the ectopic focus is usually curative for focal atrial tachycardia, in about 90%; oral beta blockers or calcium channel blockers are the initial chronic therapy.
Adenosine is a diagnostic tool that usually does not terminate focal atrial tachycardia, so it cannot cure it.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Which rhythm describes atrial fibrillation?
opts: Correct. Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves and no PR interval, usually at 110 to 160 with a narrow QRS.
A regular rhythm with sawtooth waves is atrial flutter, an organized atrial circuit.
An irregular rhythm with at least three P-wave shapes is multifocal atrial tachycardia, which still has P waves.
A regular narrow rhythm with hidden P waves is supraventricular tachycardia such as nodal reentry; atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular.

set1.q: Which type of atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia is more common?
opts: Correct. Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia is orthodromic or antidromic, and orthodromic is more common; it produces a regular, narrow complex tachycardia.
Antidromic reentry, with retrograde conduction up the node and a wide QRS, is the less common form.
Multifocal describes an atrial tachycardia from three or more foci, not a type of accessory pathway reentry.
Slow-fast is the common typical form of atrioventricular nodal reentry, not of accessory pathway reentry.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: What is the cure rate of catheter ablation for atrioventricular nodal reentry?
opts: Ablation for nodal reentry is far better than a coin flip, with a definitive cure in over 95%.
A 70% cure would undersell it; ablation for nodal reentry offers a definitive cure in over 95% of selected patients.
About 90% is the cure rate quoted for catheter ablation of focal atrial tachycardia; nodal reentry ablation exceeds 95%.
Correct. Catheter ablation offers a select subset of patients with nodal reentry the opportunity for a definitive cure, in over 95%.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: How does the rhythm of multifocal atrial tachycardia compare with focal atrial tachycardia?
opts: This reverses them: the single focus of focal atrial tachycardia gives a regular rhythm, and the several foci of multifocal give an irregular one.
Only focal atrial tachycardia is regular; multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular.
Both have one P wave for every QRS; it is atrial fibrillation that lacks P waves.
Correct. Focal atrial tachycardia is regular because one focus fires; multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular because at least three foci fire independently.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Atrioventricular block b. Bundle branch blocks c. Ventricular premature beats d. Ventricular tachycardia e. Ventricular fibrillation f. Torsades de Pointes g. Idioventricular rhythm h. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
set2.q: How do most people with premature junctional contractions present?
opts: Syncope is not the usual picture; premature junctional contractions are mostly asymptomatic.
Chest pain is not typical; most people with premature junctional beats have no symptoms.
Stroke is the embolic risk of atrial fibrillation; premature junctional beats are mostly silent.
Correct. Most people with premature junctional contractions are not symptomatic, and no treatment is needed if they are asymptomatic and infrequent; reassurance is often adequate.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: Which rhythm is listed among those that can exceed 200 beats per minute and cause collapse?
opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is an irregular rhythm of acutely ill lung or heart patients and is not among the rhythms listed for rates above 200.
Focal atrial tachycardia is generally a benign arrhythmia with abrupt palpitations; it is not one of the rhythms listed as exceeding 200.
Sinus tachycardia stays at or below about 160; the rhythms that exceed 200 are the reentry tachycardias and pre-excited atrial fibrillation.
Correct. Rates above 200 with syncope or collapse are seen in accessory pathway reentry, nodal reentry and atrial fibrillation with an accessory pathway (for example Wolff-Parkinson-White).

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: Which is a physiologic cause of sinus tachycardia?
opts: Correct. Pain and anxiety are physiologic causes, as is exercise; the pathologic causes include hypovolemia, shock, anemia, hypoxia, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction and hyperthyroidism.
Hypovolemia is a pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia; the physiologic causes are responses such as pain, anxiety and exercise.
Pulmonary embolism is a pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia, not a physiologic one like pain or anxiety.
Hyperthyroidism is a pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia; physiologic sinus tachycardia is the response to pain, anxiety or exercise.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: Sinus tachycardia is defined by a sinus rate in which range?
opts: A sinus rate of 60 to 100 is normal sinus rhythm; sinus tachycardia starts above 100.

Correct. Sinus tachycardia is a regular sinus rhythm above 100 up to 160 beats per minute, with a P wave for every QRS; above 160 the P waves are lost and the rhythm is called supraventricular tachycardia.
Above 160 beats per minute the P waves are hidden and the rhythm is called supraventricular tachycardia; sinus tachycardia runs from just over 100 to 160.
An atrial rate of 250 or more, approaching 300, is atrial flutter; sinus tachycardia stays between 100 and 160.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: When is catheter ablation used for premature atrial contractions?
opts: Most premature atrial contractions are benign and asymptomatic and need no treatment, let alone ablation.
Asymptomatic premature atrial contractions get no treatment; ablation is for frequent beats or those triggering fibrillation.
Premature atrial beats brought on by caffeine are managed by avoiding the trigger and reassurance; ablation is for frequent beats or those triggering atrial fibrillation.
Correct. Catheter ablation is used if premature atrial contractions are frequent or are triggering atrial fibrillation; otherwise a beta blocker or reassurance is used.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: In hemodynamically stable atrial fibrillation, what is the first aim of management?
opts: A pacemaker treats slow rhythms; stable atrial fibrillation is first rate-controlled.
Correct. Stable atrial fibrillation is managed first with rate control (intravenous if in rapid ventricular response, oral if not), with anticoagulation guided by stroke risk.
Elective conversion comes later, as outpatient cardioversion after 21 days of anticoagulation; the first aim in a stable patient is rate control.
Mapping and ablation is a later option; the first step in stable atrial fibrillation is rate control.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: Which trigger can precipitate atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia?
opts: High vagal tone slows conduction and explains bradycardia or junctional rhythm in athletes; vagal maneuvers actually terminate nodal reentry.
Correct. Nodal reentry may occur spontaneously or with exertion, caffeine, alcohol, beta-agonists or sympathomimetics, usually without heart disease.
Hypothyroidism slows the heart and causes sinus bradycardia or sick sinus syndrome; caffeine is the listed trigger for nodal reentry.
Beta blockers are used as a 'pill in the pocket' to stop nodal reentry; it is beta-agonists that can trigger it.

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
set2.q: Besides athletes and sleepers, which adult group commonly shows sinus bradycardia?
opts: Correct. Sinus bradycardia is listed as seen in adults over 65 years, as well as in well-conditioned, active people and during sleep.
Anxiety causes a physiologic sinus tachycardia, not bradycardia; sinus bradycardia is listed in adults over 65.
Hyperthyroidism speeds the sinus rate; sinus bradycardia is the finding in adults over 65 and in conditioned athletes.
Stimulants cause sinus tachycardia; the adult group listed for sinus bradycardia is those over 65.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: Which electrocardiogram pattern defines sinus arrhythmia?
opts: Irregularly irregular with no P waves
An irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves is atrial fibrillation; sinus arrhythmia keeps a normal P wave before every QRS.
A regular rhythm with sawtooth waves is atrial flutter, from a rapid atrial circuit; sinus arrhythmia has normal sinus P waves.
At least three distinct P-wave shapes in one lead with an irregular rhythm is multifocal atrial tachycardia, not the breathing-linked sinus variation.
Correct. Sinus arrhythmia is irregular with a pattern that follows breathing, at 60 to 100 beats per minute, with a uniform P wave before every narrow QRS and a normal PR interval.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: What is the first-line treatment for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia?
opts: Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, not a drug to speed a slow heart; atropine is first line.
A permanent pacemaker is definitive care for chronic symptomatic bradycardia; the acute, unstable patient first gets atropine, then a temporary pacemaker.
Correct. Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia; if it fails, a temporary pacemaker follows, and chronic symptomatic disease gets a permanent pacemaker.
Adenosine slows conduction through the atrioventricular node and is used for stable supraventricular tachycardia; it would worsen a bradycardia.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following ventricular dysrhythmias: a. Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
set2.q: Which drug is used for persistent symptoms from premature junctional contractions?
opts: Correct. If symptoms from premature junctional contractions persist, a beta blocker such as metoprolol is used if not contraindicated; reassurance of the benign rhythm is often adequate.
Adenosine terminates reentrant supraventricular tachycardia for seconds; persistent junctional beats are suppressed with a beta blocker.
Atropine speeds the sinus node in unstable bradycardia; symptomatic premature junctional beats get metoprolol.
Procainamide is for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; a beta blocker such as metoprolol treats junctional beats.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: After how much anticoagulation can stable atrial fibrillation be electively cardioverted as an outpatient?
opts: A single day of anticoagulation is not enough before elective outpatient cardioversion; 21 days are given.
Correct. Outpatient cardioversion of atrial fibrillation follows 21 days of anticoagulation; anticoagulation is guided by stroke risk throughout.
Three months is longer than needed; outpatient cardioversion can follow 21 days of anticoagulation.
A year of anticoagulation is not required first; elective cardioversion follows 21 days.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia depends on which structure?
opts: Three or more atrial foci make multifocal atrial tachycardia, an irregular rhythm without a reentry loop.
A failing sinus node is sick sinus syndrome; reentrant tachycardia needs an extra connection between atria and ventricles.
Correct. Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia is seen in patients with an accessory pathway, such as Wolff-Parkinson-White; the loop uses the atrioventricular node and the pathway.
A circuit confined to the atrioventricular node is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia, which needs no accessory pathway.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: What is the definitive management of atrial flutter?
opts: Vagal maneuvers terminate nodal reentry, not the atrial circuit of flutter, which ablation treats definitively.
Correct. Ablation is the definitive management of atrial flutter, which has a substantial recurrence rate and is harder to rate-control than fibrillation.
Adenosine may briefly slow conduction but does not cure flutter; ablation is definitive.
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms such as sick sinus syndrome; the flutter circuit is cured by ablation.

Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
set2.q: Which cardiac event is a listed cause of junctional rhythm?
opts: Hypovolemia and shock drive sinus tachycardia; junctional rhythm follows inferior infarction, surgery, sinus node failure or digoxin toxicity.
Hyperthyroidism speeds the sinus node into tachycardia; it does not let the junction take over.
Correct. Inferior myocardial infarction is a listed cause of junctional rhythm, with sinus node dysfunction, the acute period after cardiac surgery and digoxin toxicity.
Pulmonary embolism is a pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia, not junctional rhythm.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: In sick sinus syndrome, a fast run that is irregularly irregular with no P waves alternates with pauses. Which rhythm is the fast run?
opts: Sinus tachycardia is regular, with a normal P wave before every QRS; in tachy-brady syndrome the fast rhythm comes from outside the failing sinus node, most commonly atrial fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Ventricular tachycardia can be the fast rhythm in a few patients, who then need a pacemaker with a defibrillator, but it is regular and wide; an irregularly irregular run without P waves is atrial fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. An irregularly irregular fast rhythm with no P waves is atrial fibrillation, and in tachy-brady syndrome, the form of sick sinus syndrome in which fast and slow rhythms alternate, atrial fibrillation is the most common tachyarrhythmia.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular too, but every QRS has a P wave, in at least three shapes; a fast run with no P waves is atrial fibrillation, the usual fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.q: When premature junctional contractions are frequent (over 10 per minute), what is done?
opts: Correct. Frequent premature junctional contractions (more than 10 per minute, or multifocal) prompt a search for structural heart disease and treatment with a beta blocker.
Reassurance alone suits infrequent, asymptomatic junctional beats; frequent ones prompt a search for structural heart disease.
Anticoagulation is for atrial fibrillation and flutter; frequent junctional beats lead to a search for structural heart disease.
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms; frequent premature junctional beats prompt a structural workup and a beta blocker.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: In sinus arrest, which rhythm may take over?
opts: Ventricular fibrillation is disorganized activity with no pulse, not the rhythm that follows sinus arrest; that rhythm is junctional.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia comes from three or more atrial foci in acutely ill lung or heart patients; it is not the rhythm that follows sinus arrest, which is junctional.
Correct. In sinus arrest the sinus node does not generate an impulse, and a junctional rhythm may take over, often with inverted (retrograde) P waves or none visible.
Atrial flutter is a rapid atrial circuit with sawtooth waves; sinus arrest, where the sinus node generates no impulse, leads to a junctional rhythm.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: Atrial flutter is commonly seen in which patients?
opts: Raised intracranial pressure is a cause of sinus bradycardia; flutter is linked to atrial scarring and right-sided heart disease.

Correct. Atrial flutter is commonly seen with atrial scarring or damage (for example after surgery), right-sided heart failure or pulmonary vascular disease, and in atrial fibrillation patients taking an antiarrhythmic.
Caffeine in young women is the classic setting of atrioventricular nodal reentry; flutter follows atrial scarring or right-sided disease.
Conditioned athletes show sinus bradycardia or junctional rhythm from vagal tone; flutter needs atrial damage or right-sided disease.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: Which is a recognized cause of sick sinus syndrome?
opts: Caffeine is a trigger for atrioventricular nodal reentry and premature atrial beats; it is not a listed cause of sick sinus syndrome.
Correct. Causes of sick sinus syndrome include sinoatrial node ischemia, injury to the node from cardiac surgery, electrolyte abnormalities, medications and hypothyroidism.
It is hypothyroidism that is listed as a cause of sick sinus syndrome; excess thyroid hormone speeds the sinus rate instead.
Anemia drives a compensatory sinus tachycardia; the listed causes of sick sinus syndrome are node ischemia or surgical injury, electrolytes, drugs and hypothyroidism.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: What is the management of asymptomatic sinus bradycardia?
opts: Correct. Asymptomatic sinus bradycardia needs no treatment; atropine is for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia and a permanent pacemaker for chronic symptomatic disease.
Atropine is first line only for acute, symptomatic and hemodynamically unstable bradycardia; an asymptomatic patient is left untreated.
A temporary pacemaker follows atropine in an unstable, symptomatic patient; it has no place when the bradycardia causes no symptoms.
A permanent pacemaker is for chronic, symptomatic bradycardia; asymptomatic sinus bradycardia is not treated.

set2.q: What does a premature junctional contraction look like?
opts: Early narrow QRS, P inverted or hidden
Correct. A premature junctional contraction gives an early narrow QRS with either an inverted P wave, a P wave buried in the QRS (no P visible) or a P wave after the QRS.
Early wide QRS without a P wave
An early, wide and bizarre QRS with no P wave is a premature ventricular contraction.
An early, abnormally shaped P wave before a narrow QRS is a premature atrial contraction.
Sawtooth waves belong to atrial flutter; a junctional beat has an inverted, buried or following P wave.

Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: Which type of atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia is most common?
opts: Orthodromic is the more common form of accessory pathway reentry, not a type of nodal reentry.
Antidromic is the less common, wide-complex form of accessory pathway reentry, not a nodal reentry type.
Correct. Slow-fast (typical) is the most common type of atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia, a regular narrow complex tachycardia with hidden P waves.
Fast-slow reverses the usual direction around the node and is the less common pattern; slow-fast is the most common type of atrioventricular nodal reentry.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: How do patients with atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia most commonly present?
opts: Correct. Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia is seen in patients with an accessory pathway, and they most commonly present with palpitations.
Stroke is the embolic complication that anticoagulation prevents in atrial fibrillation; reentrant tachycardia most often presents with palpitations.
Heart failure is not the usual presentation of reentrant tachycardia; patients most commonly present with palpitations.
Reentry through an accessory pathway produces a tachycardia, typically felt as palpitations, not a slow rhythm.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: In a stable narrow complex tachycardia, which step comes before any drug?
opts: Correct. A vagal maneuver is first line for stable supraventricular (narrow complex) tachycardia, before adenosine; synchronized cardioversion is kept for instability.
Imaging does not terminate the rhythm; in a stable narrow complex tachycardia the first step is a vagal maneuver.
Procainamide is reserved for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; the first step in stable narrow complex tachycardia is a vagal maneuver.
Synchronized cardioversion is immediate treatment only when the patient is unstable; a stable patient starts with a vagal maneuver.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atrial and supraventricular dysrhythmias: a. Sinus arrhythmia b. Sinus bradycardia c. Sinus tachycardia d. Sick sinus syndrome e. Atrial premature beats f. Atrial flutter g. Atrial fibrillation h. Atrial tachycardia i. Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set2.q: What is a delta wave?
opts: An inverted T wave is a repolarization change; the delta wave is the slurred upstroke at the beginning of the QRS complex.
A sawtooth baseline is the flutter wave of atrial flutter; the delta wave is a slurred QRS upstroke.
A slurred upstroke of the QRS
Correct. The delta wave is a slurred upstroke of the QRS complex, seen with a short PR interval and a widened QRS in Wolff-Parkinson-White.
A notched or widened P wave is an atrial finding; the delta wave is a slurred start to the QRS from early ventricular activation.

set2.q: Which pair are both listed risk factors for atrial fibrillation?
opts: Older age, not youth, is the listed age risk; female sex is not on the list of atrial fibrillation risks.
Obesity, not low weight, is a listed risk; anemia drives sinus tachycardia instead.
Correct. Hypertension and diabetes are both listed, along with cardiac disease, family history, obesity, sleep apnea, excessive alcohol and older age.
Neither is a listed risk: hypothyroidism slows the sinus rate, and it is high blood pressure (hypertension), not low, that sits on the list with diabetes.

set2.q: An irregular, wide-complex tachycardia with some rates approaching 300 appears in someone with a known accessory pathway. Which intravenous drug is used?
opts: Adenosine must never be used here: it blocks only the normal node and lets the accessory pathway conduct the fibrillation at rates approaching 300.
Atropine speeds conduction and is used for unstable bradycardia; it would make a pre-excited tachycardia faster, not slower.
Intravenous magnesium breaks torsades de pointes; pre-excited atrial fibrillation is treated with procainamide.

Correct. An irregular, wide-complex tachycardia approaching 300 with an accessory pathway is atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White (ventricular tachycardia would be regular at 150 to 200), treated with intravenous procainamide, never adenosine.
